w: What's tested Dr. Herr's study guide for this lecture: the common disorders of the vulva, vagina and cervix; telling neoplastic lesions from non-neoplastic ones; the important infectious causes (infectious vaginitis: Candida and Trichomonas; HPV); the relationship between HPV and cervical neoplasia; and the age-related patterns of the tumors (sarcoma botryoides in little girls, squamous cell carcinoma in women of reproductive age, the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma and the aggressive endometrial carcinoma in older women). Key terms: lichen sclerosus, condyloma acuminatum, sarcoma botryoides, HPV, cervical neoplasia, infectious vaginitis The cervix's transformation zone, where the glandular and squamous epithelia meet and "fight": constantly inflamed, open to HPV infection, and where cervical cancer arises; the precursors (low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions), 90 percent linked to HPV, and the koilocyte Lichen sclerosus, where Dr. Dal Zotto paused "because this is important": the non-infectious inflammatory disorder she said can lead to carcinoma (her slide lists lichen planus beside it), the HPV-independent squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva in older women Lichen planus, "because you're going to be dentists": vulvar and oral lesions together point to it The endometrium's two carcinomas, the leiomyoma (very common, abnormal bleeding), and the breast: ductal versus lobular carcinoma, in situ versus invasive, Paget disease of the nipple, the receptors (estrogen, progesterone, HER2) and gynecomastia What the lecture said you don't need: the details of the new cervical screening (know only that management is now risk-based), the classification of ovarian tumors (know that most are epithelial, and that ovarian cancer is lethal), and how ductal and lobular carcinoma in situ differ under the microscope 1 HPV and cervical neoplasia: cancer arises in the transformation zone, where the glandular and squamous epithelia "fight" and stay inflamed and open to HPV; the precursors are squamous intraepithelial lesions, low grade (CIN1, can regress) or high grade (CIN2 and CIN3, progress), about 90 percent HPV-linked (and more than 90 percent of cervical cancers), marked by the koilocyte, in situ until they invade the stroma Study guide + recording + slides · 11 questions in the bank Know this Cervical cancer arises in the transformation zone, where the endocervix's glandular epithelium meets the ectocervix's squamous epithelium. The fighting of epithelia keeps the transformation zone inflamed and open to HPV, which can progress to carcinoma. Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions can regress; high-grade ones progress. About 90 percent are linked to HPV. Where the two epithelia meet is the transformation zone, the junction of the epithelia. Through the reproductive years the glandular epithelium of the endocervix tries to grow out onto the ectocervix and the squamous epithelium tries to grow into the canal: they collide, "what we call the fighting of epithelia." So the transformation zone is constantly inflamed and injured, and that chronic inflammation makes it susceptible to infection, above all HPV, the virus that affects the whole genital tract in women and men. That is why the transformation zone is where cervical cancer arises. The slide: HPV causes more than 90 percent of cervical cancers. The precursors of cervical cancer are squamous intraepithelial lesions (SIL; also called cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN), because they affect the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix, as penile intraepithelial lesions do on the penis. They are low grade (LSIL, or CIN1), which progress slowly and can regress, or high grade (HSIL: CIN2 and CIN3), which are less likely to regress and more likely to progress to carcinoma. About 90 percent are linked to HPV, in the reproductive years; the slide notes that more than 40 HPV types are involved. 2 Lichen sclerosus, where the lecture paused "because this is important": an atrophic epithelium over dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, a parchment-like vulva; the non-infectious inflammatory disorder the lecture said leads to carcinoma, the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women (her slide lists lichen planus beside it); the HPV-associated kind is HPV 16 in more than 70 percent Study guide + recording + slides · 6 questions in the bank The epithelium is completely atrophic, and the hallmark is extensive dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, pink material in the dermis. The vulva looks very smooth, like parchment paper or cellophane (the slide: white plaques with a "wrinkled parchment" look, very itchy). Lichen sclerosus itches, so the patient scratches, and lichen simplex chronicus can form on top of it. "Lichen sclerosus is the single non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinomas." HPV-associated: from HPV 16 and 18 ("bigger numbers"; the slide: HPV 16 in more than 70 percent); a better progression-free survival, and radiosensitive. The slide's stain for it is p16. HPV-independent: in older women, over 60, associated with lichen sclerosus (the slide: "lichen sclerosus or lichen planus", long-standing inflammation). That is why lichen sclerosus has to be diagnosed in time and treated, not left until a squamous cell carcinoma develops. 3 Infectious vaginitis: Candida (pseudohyphae, little sticks, a lot of inflammation) and Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan that looks like a squamous cell with prolongations), against non-infectious atrophic vaginitis in older women Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this Infectious vaginitis: Candida (pseudohyphae, little sticks) and Trichomonas vaginalis (a sexually transmitted protozoan with prolongations). Non-infectious: atrophic vaginitis in older women. Candida, a fungus: its pseudohyphae look like "little sticks" in the cytology, with a lot of inflammation; very frequent. Trichomonas vaginalis, a sexually transmitted protozoan, a very common cause of vaginitis: easy to diagnose in cytology, because it looks like a squamous cell but has cytoplasmic prolongations (pseudopods). Atrophic vaginitis, non-infectious, very common in older women, not related to any infectious agent. 4 Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types; benign, finger-like and wart-like, with koilocytes, anywhere on the anogenital tract; less common since the HPV vaccine Study guide + recording + slides · 3 questions in the bank Know this Condyloma acuminatum: HPV 6 and 11, benign, finger-like and wart-like, with koilocytes. Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: HPV 16 and 18 (16 in more than 70 percent, the slide), or, in women over 60, lichen sclerosus (the slide adds lichen planus). As on the penis, condyloma acuminatum can affect any part of the anogenital tract. It is associated with HPV 6 and 11, the low-risk types: a benign condition, though it can be painful or ulcerate. It forms finger-like, exophytic, wart-like (verruciform) lesions, big or small, and under the microscope it shows koilocytes, because it is HPV. It is sexually transmitted, and the slide notes that it is getting less common since the HPV vaccine. 5 The age patterns of the tumors: sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) in girls under 5, with a good prognosis if treated in time; squamous cell carcinomas in women of reproductive age; the HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma and the aggressive serous and clear cell endometrial carcinomas in older women (70 to 80 on the slide) Study guide + recording + slides · 5 questions in the bank Know this Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) in girls under 5, with a good prognosis if treated in time; squamous cell carcinomas in women of reproductive age. In very young girls, under 5, a different tumor is prevalent: sarcoma botryoides, an embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, a very primitive tumor. It has a good prognosis if it is found in time and treated with surgery and chemotherapy. "So know that there are certain tumors that affect the girls, and usually the squamous cell carcinomas affect the women in reproductive age." Girls under 5 Sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma) of the vagina Women of reproductive age Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and vagina, HPV-related; endometrioid adenocarcinoma in younger women (45 to 65) with excess estrogen Older women HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (over 60, lichen sclerosus); the aggressive serous and clear cell carcinomas of the endometrium (over 65; the slide, 70 to 80) 6 The common disorders of the vulva, and neoplastic versus non-neoplastic: lichen simplex chronicus (thickened, leathery, from scratching), lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are inflammatory; squamous intraepithelial lesions, VaIN, squamous cell carcinoma, clear cell adenocarcinoma and sarcoma botryoides are neoplastic Study guide + recording + slides · 4 questions in the bank Know this From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Dal Zotto's lecture. Know HPV and the cervix (the transformation zone, the low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions, 90 percent HPV, the koilocyte), the infectious vaginitis pair (Candida's pseudohyphae; Trichomonas, a sexually transmitted protozoan with prolongations) against atrophic vaginitis, the vulva's lichens (lichen sclerosus leads to HPV-independent carcinoma; the slide adds lichen planus), condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6 and 11, benign), and the ages: sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5, squamous carcinomas in the reproductive years, lichen sclerosus carcinoma in older women. A thickening of the vulvar skin (a squamous mucosa) from continuous scratching and rubbing. In older patients, an atrophic epithelium with less estrogen becomes itchy and the patient scratches; or a psychological problem leads to scratching. The epithelium thickens, with hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis and acanthosis, and the skin looks leathery. It is a reaction to many conditions that cause pruritus. Cervix Inflammation of the transformation zone Low- and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions; squamous cell carcinoma Vagina Vaginitis: Candida, Trichomonas, atrophic Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia, squamous cell carcinoma, clear cell adenocarcinoma; sarcoma botryoides in girls under 5 Vulva Lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus; condyloma acuminatum (a benign HPV lesion) Squamous intraepithelial lesions; squamous cell carcinoma (HPV 16 and 18, or lichen sclerosus and, on the slide, lichen planus) 7 Lichen planus, "because you're going to be dentists": vulvar and oral erosions together, with a white, lace-like pattern; a band of lymphocytes under the epithelium; a fresh biopsy (not formalin) for immunofluorescence, which shows shaggy fibrin at the dermoepidermal junction; steroids Recording + slides · 3 questions in the bank Know this Lichen planus: oral and vulvar erosions together; a fresh biopsy (not in formalin) for immunofluorescence; steroids. "You must know about this, because you're going to be dentists." Lichen planus is an inflammatory disorder of the oral mucosa and also of the vulva, where its diagnosis is often delayed because it isn't recognized. If a patient has vulvar and oral lesions, it is most likely lichen planus. It is postulated to be an autoimmune, T-cell-mediated disorder; the slide puts it in women of 30 to 60 and describes a white, lace-like pattern with redness. It causes erosions, sometimes very painful and ulcerated, in the vulva and the mouth, with many inflammatory cells, especially lymphocytes, in the dermis: on the slide, hyperkeratosis and hypergranulosis, a band-like infiltrate of lymphocytes under the epithelium, and vacuolization of the basal layer. The diagnosis is easy: send the biopsy to the pathology laboratory fresh, not in formalin, for immunofluorescence, which shows no immune complexes and a deposit of fibrin: on the slide, "shaggy" fibrin along the dermoepidermal junction. The patient is treated with steroids. 8 Cervical cancer and its prevention: fourth in women worldwide (breast is first), less common in the United States thanks to Pap screening (a fourth of women lack access), the HPV vaccine (decades to show its full benefit), and management now based on each patient's risk; over a lifetime up to 5 percent of unscreened women develop it, under 0.5 percent with screening and treatment Recording + slides · 4 questions in the bank Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in women worldwide; breast cancer is first. It is less frequent in the United States because screening (Papanicolaou cytology, the Pap test) finds the premalignant lesions early and is well established and widespread. Still, about a fourth of U.S. women can't get or don't have access to screening, and over a lifetime cervical cancer develops in up to 5 percent of women who aren't screened. Effective screening reduces both the incidence and the mortality significantly: the slide says screening and treating the precancers bring the lifetime risk under 0.5 percent. Its other numbers: 11.5 cases a year per 100,000 U.S. women, and more than 4,000 deaths a year, mostly because precancers weren't found and treated. 9 The two endometrial carcinomas, "just know": endometrioid adenocarcinoma (estrogen excess, obesity, estrogen without progesterone; well differentiated, less aggressive, younger women) and the aggressive serous and clear cell carcinomas of women over 65 (70 to 80 on the slide), not hormone-related; endometrioid arises in hyperplasia with atypia Recording + slides · 4 questions in the bank Know this Endometrioid adenocarcinoma: estrogen excess (obesity, estrogen without progesterone), well differentiated, less aggressive, younger women. The other type (the slide: serous and clear cell carcinoma, 70 to 80, not hormone-related): over 65, unlike endometrium, more aggressive. Endometrioid adenocarcinoma, which looks somewhat like normal endometrium (hence the name): tied to estrogen stimulation, in obese patients with excess estrogen or women taking estrogen without progesterone to counteract it. It arises in a background of endometrial hyperplasia with atypia (the slide), is well differentiated and less aggressive, and the patients are younger: 45 to 65 on the slide (the lecture said premenopausal or perimenopausal). 10 Breast carcinoma: DCIS needs treatment, LCIS is now considered benign; invasive ductal carcinoma forms glands, invasive lobular grows in single files; Paget disease of the nipple means a carcinoma underneath; the prognosis rests on size, nodes and the estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2; of the benign lesions, atypical ductal hyperplasia carries the most risk Recording + slides · 8 questions in the bank Know this Breast carcinoma's prognosis: type, size, lymph nodes, and the estrogen and progesterone receptors and HER2, which drugs can target; anti-estrogen therapy for an estrogen-receptor tumor. Like any carcinoma, breast carcinoma is in situ or invasive. The carcinomas in situ: ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), from the ducts; lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), from the lobules; and Paget disease of the nipple. The WHO now considers LCIS a benign lesion, neoplastic but benign, and no treatment is needed. DCIS needs treatment, usually surgery, with or without radiotherapy, and it has a good prognosis. (How they differ under the microscope: "you don't need to know that.") The prognosis of an invasive breast carcinoma depends on its histologic type (ductal or lobular), its size, its grade (on the slide: the nuclear grade, tubule formation and the mitotic count), lymphovascular invasion, the presence of lymph node metastases and distant disease (the stage), and whether it expresses estrogen or progesterone receptors and the surface protein HER2. All of them can be targeted by specific drugs, so knowing a tumor's receptor and HER2 status guides the treatment: complete surgical excision, external beam radiation, with or without chemotherapy, anti-estrogen therapy (tamoxifen) for a tumor that expresses estrogen receptors, and breast reconstruction. 11 Chronic endometritis and the leiomyoma: plasma cells in the endometrium, a common cause of infertility treated with antibiotics; the leiomyoma, very common, a well-circumscribed nodule that makes the uterus bleed, against the aggressive leiomyosarcoma that spreads to the lung; the leiomyosarcoma is infiltrative, with increased mitoses, atypia or necrosis Recording + slides · 4 questions in the bank The leiomyoma is the benign tumor of the uterine smooth muscle, and it is very frequent: the lecture said nearly every woman has some by perimenopause or after. Leiomyomas are white, elastic, very well-circumscribed nodules in the myometrium, and under the microscope they have no mitoses, atypia or necrosis (the slide). "It's like having a foreign body in the midst of the myometrium": the myometrium can't contract well, so the usual symptom is excess, abnormal uterine bleeding. The malignant one, the leiomyosarcoma, is very aggressive and can metastasize to the lung very easily. The slide's contrast: it is infiltrative, not well circumscribed, with increased mitoses, atypia or necrosis. Behavior Benign, very frequent Malignant, very aggressive Edge Well circumscribed Infiltrative Microscope No mitoses, atypia or necrosis Increased mitoses, atypia or necrosis Symptom or spread Abnormal uterine bleeding Metastasizes to the lung 12 The ovary and the male breast: most ovarian tumors are epithelial, and ovarian cancer is lethal; gynecomastia (aromatase in fat, testosterone in weightlifters) is far more common than male breast cancer, which has no screening; stage for stage, a man's breast cancer has the same prognosis as a woman's (BRCA2 in some) Recording + slides · 5 questions in the bank Know this Most ovarian tumors are epithelial, from the surface; ovarian cancer is aggressive and lethal. The ovary gives rise to a plethora of tumors; the classification isn't needed ("Don't shoot me. I don't need you to know this"). Know that most ovarian tumors come from the surface epithelium (the epithelial tumors; the slide: 95 percent of ovarian cancers); others come from the germ cells (the germ cell tumors, as in the testis) and from the stroma. Ovarian cancer is lethal: it causes more deaths than its frequency would suggest, it is very aggressive, it needs a lot of chemotherapy and debulking surgery, and the prognosis isn't good. The male breast has the same pathology as the female breast, but its cancer is found later, because men have no mammography or screening: the cancer is so rare that a screening program isn't justified. So it is usually advanced when it is found, but stage for stage its prognosis is the same as a woman's, and the patient may have a family history (BRCA2), the slide adds. Much more common is gynecomastia, an enlarged breast from a relative excess of estrogen: in obese men, whose fat has the aromatase that converts testosterone to estradiol, and in weightlifters who take testosterone. Also flagged in class The koilocyte, a bigger nucleus with a clear halo around it, is HPV's mark in cytology and biopsies. High-grade cells: less cytoplasm, a higher N:C ratio, pleomorphic nuclei. Lichen sclerosus: atrophic epithelium, dermal sclerosis and hyalinization, a parchment-like vulva; it leads to the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of older women. Of the three lichens, lichen sclerosus is the one she said leads to carcinoma. Her slide on vulvar carcinoma lists lichen planus beside it ("lichen sclerosus or lichen planus", long-standing inflammation), so know lichen sclerosus first without calling lichen planus risk-free. Chronic endometritis: plasma cells in the endometrial stroma, a common cause of infertility, treated with antibiotics. Paget disease of the nipple, a scaly red nipple of carcinoma cells, means looking for the carcinoma underneath. You can skip Skip the screening slide's details; know that cervical screening and management are now risk-based. Skip the classification of ovarian tumors; know that most are epithelial (then germ cell and stromal) and that ovarian cancer is lethal. Skip how DCIS and LCIS differ under the microscope; know that DCIS needs treatment and LCIS is now considered benign.
